2610.36619.abstract: Zr cladding alloys in nuclear reactors are exposed to high neutron fluxes, making irradiation-induced defects and solute segregation central to understanding their in-service behaviour. Dislocation cores involve short-range chemistry and long-range elastic fields, which are difficult to describe simultaneously using conventional atomistic methods. Using a hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning (QM/ML) framework, this part of work examines prismatic <a> loops in hcp α-Zr. All three loop variants are considered, including faulted and perfect, interstitial- and vacancy-type, and first- and second-order prismatic configurations. Nine possible dislocation line segments are characterised in terms of core geometry, solute binding, glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transition pathways using QM/ML and newly implemented QM/ML-NEB calculations. Shockley and half-Shockley partials, together with basal and prismatic fault ribbons, are found to govern core stabilisation. Fe and H preferentially bind to faulted segments, whereas Sn and Nb favour perfect segments. Solutes can also drive partial motion, recombination and local unfaulting. These results establish a comprehensive picture of <a> loop microstructure, solute trapping and transition mechanisms in α-Zr.
2610.36619.title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in α-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers
topics: Atomistic Modeling of Sulfides and Minerals

2610.36659.abstract: Anion redox in Li-rich layered oxides places holes on oxygen next to an antiferromagnetic Mn(IV) d3 lattice, a strongly correlated open-shell problem for which projection-based wavefunction-in-DFT embedding offers a route to correlated and quantum solvers, but whose errors are known mainly for closed-shell molecules. We develop a spin-unrestricted projection-based embedding, exact at the DFT-in-DFT level to the microhartree scale for closed-shell, broken-symmetry and high-spin references with point charges, and apply DMRG-in-DFT to point-charge clusters of delithiated Li(2-x)MnO3, varying the environment functional (0-100% exact exchange), geometry, active region, active-space spin, virtual space, cluster size and magnetic reference. In every setting the lowest SCF state places the hole on an oxygen pair, with no O-O bond. How the hole is shared depends on the functional together with the geometry: hybrids give a full, uncoupled hole at the DFT+U geometry but a partial, weakly covalent hole at their own geometry, a change of up to 0.5 e on one oxygen. Where spin spreads across the active/environment boundary, the integer spin projection of the active space becomes a choice worth up to 0.26 e, and at most 0.09 e once the two Mn neighbors are included. An extended state search found missed lower states for two functionals, changing a pair-oxygen spin by up to 0.45 e. Across all 82 runs the embedded mean field gives the same hole (median DMRG change 0.02-0.04 e); correlation mainly adds O-O covalency. State control and geometry consistency, not the solver, dominate the uncertainty, and total energies are not converged at 30-40 orbitals. For quantum solvers, the embedded Hamiltonian must be spin-unrestricted: a shared-orbital form reverses the hole, while sample-based quantum diagonalization reproduces exact diagonalization, as accurately as, but not better than, classical selected CI.
2610.36659.title: Where Does the Anion-Redox Hole Go? Reliability of Open-Shell Projection-Based Embedding for Li-Rich Cathodes, from DFT Environments to Quantum Solvers

2610.36860.abstract: Transition-metal-based batteries rely on critical elements such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Their extraction creates environmental and supply-chain challenges. Organic electrode materials (OEMs) reduce this reliance and provide broad molecular tunability. However, OEM-based batteries still show limited long-term cycling stability. Their design also requires the joint optimization of coupled metrics such as voltage, specific capacity, capacity retention, and energy density. These metrics depend on the full battery stack and on the interactions among its components rather than on the active material alone. In our previous work, we developed a data-fusion multi-task framework for average discharge voltage and first-cycle specific capacity. Both targets are single-valued. Here, we extend that framework to multi-horizon prediction by predicting a property at every cycle of a discharge trajectory rather than at a single cycle. Our multi-fidelity and Multi-horizon Deep Operator Network learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories within one model. We train it on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions, so it learns battery-stack interactions rather than cathode-only effects. This framework supports long-term property prediction, inverse design, and process optimization for organic battery systems.
2610.36860.title: HorizON: A Multi-Horizon Deep Operator Network for Property Prediction of Organic Battery Stacks

2610.37095.abstract: Opening a band gap in metallic two-dimensional carbon allotropes is an important step toward their use in electronic and optoelectronic devices, and full hydrogenation has proven to be an effective route to achieve it. Here, we propose irida-graphane, the fully hydrogenated derivative of the irida-graphene, a monolayer composed of three-, six-, and eight-membered rings, and investigate its structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory (DFT) at the PBE and HSE06 levels combined with phonon and \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. All carbon atoms adopt $sp^3$ hybridization, with the hydrogen atoms of the three- and six-membered rings bonded to opposite sides of a buckled carbon framework, and the lattice parameter contracts by 4.3% with respect to irida-graphene. The hydrogenation energy of $-0.53$ eV/H indicates that the hydrogenation of irida-graphene from molecular hydrogen is exothermic. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies confirms the dynamical stability of irida-graphane, and AIMD simulations show that its structure remains intact at temperatures up to 2000 K. Irida-graphane is mechanically isotropic, with an in-plane stiffness of approximately 156 N/m, a Poisson's ratio of approximately 0.1, and critical strains of approximately 20%. Hydrogenation transforms the metallic parent structure into a semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 4.68 eV (PBE) and 6.0 eV (HSE06). Irida-graphane is transparent in the visible range, with reflectivity below 0.3%, and absorbs strongly in the deep ultraviolet, with absorption coefficients of the order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ cm$^{-1}$. These results suggest irida-graphane as a candidate wide-gap material for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.
2610.37095.title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene

2610.37152.abstract: Vertically-aligned MoS$_2$ films paired with a Cu top electrode have been used as electrochemical metallization cell memristor devices. The memristive switching has been attributed to the formation of conductive filaments, yet their exact structure has remained elusive. Here we carry out a multi-scale computational study of Cu intercalation, clustering, and field-driven dynamics to eventually model the filament formation under operating conditions. We use density-functional theory results to fine-tune a machine learning force field, and the most important physical phenomena are further distilled into multi-particle kinetic Monte Carlo simulations. By exhaustive enumeration of Cu intercalated structures, we find the most stable structure at MoS$_2$Cu$_{0.11}$ composition, with Cu atoms forming a dice lattice between the MoS$_2$ layers. These structures are shown to exhibit metallic character and can thus form conductive filaments under memristor operation. The simulated switching speed and threshold voltage agree well with the available experimental data. Our results give fundamental insights on the device operation mechanism and guidelines for maximizing switching speed and endurance.
2610.37152.title: Cu intercalation and field-driven filament formation in vertically aligned MoS$_2$ memristors
topics: Atomistic Modeling of Sulfides and Minerals

2610.37483.abstract: StudDFT is a quantum chemistry program for Hartree--Fock (HF), density functional theory (DFT), and second-order Møller--Plesset (MP2) calculations of small and medium-sized molecules. It is intended primarily for teaching and student research, but its accuracy suffices for routine research calculations. Version 1.30.2 implements the RHF/UHF, RKS/UKS, and RMP2/UMP2/PUMP2 schemes in Gaussian basis sets, including effective core potentials (ECP); LDA, GGA (BLYP, BP86, BPW91, PBE), meta-GGA (r$^2$SCAN), global hybrid (B3LYP, PBE0) and range-separated hybrid ($ω$B97, $ω$B97X, $ω$B97X-D) functionals; analytical gradients and Hessians; geometry optimization, transition-state and reaction-path (IRC) searches, potential energy surface scans, harmonic frequencies and IR intensities, thermochemistry, counterpoise corrections, D3(BJ) dispersion, polarizable continuum solvation, density fitting (RI-J/RI-JK), linear-response TDDFT, and fractional-occupation smearing. The program has been verified against ORCA and PySCF on 50 molecules (30 for optimizations): the mean absolute deviations of the single-point energies do not exceed 7 $μ$Ha for HF, MP2, and the LDA, GGA, and global hybrid functionals except PBE and PBE0, whose systematic shifts of several tens of $μ$Ha are traced mainly to the value of $μ$ in the PBE exchange; those of the optimized interatomic distances and harmonic frequencies do not exceed 1.2$\times$10$^{-4}$ Å and 1.2 cm$^{-1}$. Corrections made since the first public version (0.82), mainly affecting vibrational frequencies, are documented with their effect on the verification results. Unlike large multi-language packages, StudDFT is a monolithic Fortran code with OpenMP parallelization, which simplifies its use in courses. Binaries for Windows and Linux, the documentation, and all test inputs and outputs are freely available.
2610.37483.title: StudDFT: A quantum chemistry program for educational and research purposes
topics: Electrochemical Interfaces and Solvation

2610.37606.abstract: The behavior of biomolecular complexes is governed by chemically specific interactions and often involves rare events that atomistic molecular dynamics struggle to capture within accessible timescales. Here we introduce AMARO v2.0, a coarse-grained neural network potential that retains all heavy atoms and treats solvent implicitly. Hydrogen-aware bead types and total-charge conditioning provide a shared representation for proteins, drug-like molecules, and their complexes, including ternary protein-protein-ligand systems. The model preserves folded proteins and captures key features of protein conformational free-energy landscapes. Across 262 complexes spanning 11 targets, the learned potential retains most ligand poses, although quaternary structure reorientation is observed for the HIF2A ternary complex. In targeted case studies, AMARO v2.0 distinguishes the two protonation states of trypsin-benzamidine and reaches the crystal binding pose in 3.3-fold more trajectories than all-atom molecular mechanics at a fixed estimated GPU-time budget. The same framework also recovers a reference binding pose in TYK2 and supports binding free-energy estimation for both trypsin-benzamidine and TYK2-EJM31, although the resulting values are more energetically favorable than the experimental references. SHP2 and CDK8 systems expose remaining limitations in binding-pose recovery and site specificity, respectively. Together, these results support AMARO v2.0 as a shared heavy-atom potential for biomolecular complex dynamics.
2610.37606.title: A unified coarse-grained neural network potential for the dynamics of biomolecular complexes
topics: Machine-Learned Potentials for Sulfides and Minerals

2610.37839.abstract: We present an end-to-end resource estimation of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, from its mathematical description to the allocation and scheduling of physical qubits on a chip layout. We review modern versions of Shor's algorithm for RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP, and make their logical circuits and trade-offs explicit. We compile the dominant subroutines down to physical-qubit operations on two architectures: one based on repetition cat codes and one on LDPC cat codes. We design a parity-Cnot gate for cat qubits, extend a multi-target Cnot gate to the LDPC-cat architecture, and adapt an active injection procedure to cat qubits. Building on these primitives, we adapt to cat qubits the adder from Gidney's 2025 resource estimate for factoring RSA-2048. We combine our adder compilation and a coarser estimate for the phaseup with the factory designs and lookup compilation from the FeMoco resource estimation of Kroell et al. Together, these lead to chip layouts and schedules for factoring RSA-2048.   Assuming a 1$μ$s error-correction cycle time, a 10$μ$s reaction time, circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ and no bit-flips, factoring RSA-2048, the configuration we compile in full, requires about 23 000 cat qubits and 3.14 days. Reusing the compiled operations, solving ECDLP on secp256k1 requires at most 30 000 cat qubits and 1 hour, and FFDLP-512, which we propose as an intermediate benchmark, about 6 700 cat qubits and 21 minutes. Trading space for time, RSA-2048 runs in 1.25 hours on about 611 000 cat qubits. The no-bit-flip requirement (a bit-flip time of about 100 years) can be relaxed to a bit-flip time of about one hour by adding a concatenation layer with a distance-3 bit-flip code, in which case RSA-2048 needs about 45 000 cat qubits.
2610.37839.title: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days
topics: Origin of Life and Prebiotic Mineral Catalysis

2610.37840.abstract: We provide a detailed resource estimate of the state-of-the-art sum-of-squares block encoding algorithm for electronic structure Hamiltonians of Low et al. on superconducting cat qubits. To achieve this, we present compilations with closed-form costs of the dominant subroutines such as skew-tree Qrom, a Swap network and a Phaseup for both a repetition-cat and an LDPC-cat architecture. Our compilation represents algorithmic qubits in the $X$ basis, taking advantage of the asymmetric cost of $X$ and $Z$ access that the concatenation of cat qubits with phase-flip classical code brings. Additionally, we provide a protocol for $\vert i \rangle$-state distillation and a two-level Toffoli-like $\vert \text{C}_X\text{C}_X X \rangle$ magic state distillation protocol, including three factory layouts. To minimize the cost of Clifford corrections induced by magic state injections we tailor injection gadgets to each subroutine. Combining our compilation work with the adder compilation from the companion work Pappalardo et al., we provide global layouts for the block encoding in both architectures which we use to obtain resource estimates for ground-state energy estimation for the benchmarks of FeMoco-54 and FeMoco-76. Assuming a cycle time of 1$μ$s, a reaction time of 10$\mathrmμ$s, a phase estimation precision of 1 mHa and circuit-level phase-flip noise with probability $p_Z = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ with negligible bit-flip error, FeMoco-54 requires fewer than $7\,500$ cat qubits with an expected runtime of under one day for a single phase estimation run using an LDPC-cat architecture. Relaxing the bit-flip requirement to $p_X = 10^{-11}$ with an additional layer of elevator codes raises this to an estimated $13\,000$ cat qubits.
2610.37840.title: Ground-state energy estimation compiled on cat qubits: 7 164 qubits for FeMoco-54 in 23.5 hours
topics: Origin of Life and Prebiotic Mineral Catalysis

2610.37847.abstract: Givens rotations with angles stored in quantum registers account for much of the cost of published quantum phase estimation algorithms based on double-factorized tensor hypercontraction and spectral amplification. These rotations create superpositions and cannot be verified directly by the basis-state evaluators used to optimize classical reversible circuits. We give an exact verification method that separates out a fixed Clifford change of basis and tracks basis states and phases in the remaining circuit. Integer conditions establish correctness of the full coherent action, including measurement-based uncomputation and restoration of the phase-gradient resource state. Under our interpretation of Low et al.'s angle grid and rotation convention, simplifying the adders lowers the rotation cost relative to the published accounting; fusing the two additions into one masked addition gives an additional saving. We verify both implementations exhaustively at every precision used in the published walks and prove the fused circuit correct for all widths. For benchmarks including FeMoco and other iron-sulfur clusters, replacing only the rotation term lowers total phase-estimation Toffoli counts by 9.5-14.3% under the published error budget, with the walk operator unchanged.
2610.37847.title: Exact verification of Givens rotation circuits for efficient quantum phase estimation of iron-sulfur clusters
topics: Origin of Life and Prebiotic Mineral Catalysis

2610.38236.abstract: Chemical kinetics determines molecular stability, reaction selectivity and the evolution of reacting mixtures, but discovering the underlying reaction networks remains challenging. Here we introduce ReactNexus, a generative framework for kinetic-guided network exploration starting solely from reactant graphs. Generative models propose transition states and predict the full reaction trajectories connecting reactants and products, while calculations using a machine-learned interatomic potential verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers. On an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connect to the input reactant after density functional theory (DFT) optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification. The resulting networks uncover lower-barrier cooperative pathways and competition between catalyst release and catalyst-bound branches. In the examined carbocation cascades, coverage of known product precursors saturates after limited expansion and distinct entries converge onto shared intermediates, indicating a compact accessible reaction space. Network-derived candidate structures further assist mass-spectral interpretation of a complex nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Together, these results establish a generative approach to reaction-network discovery and mechanistic analysis without predefined products or reaction templates.
2610.38236.title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks

2610.38534.abstract: Free energies of solvation are crucial to our understanding of chemical reactions, particularly when these take place in water. However, computing changes in free energies associated with the process of immersing arbitrary molecules in an aqueous solution both accurately and efficiently with the use of one universal method remains challenging. By means of atomic decompositions of total (bulk) energies from Kohn-Sham density functional theory in a basis of spatially localized molecular orbitals, the present study enables the computation of hydration free energies from local electronic-structure objects derived in the condensed phase. Specifically, our protocol computes an enthalpy of hydration as the sum of the decomposed change in internal energy of a solute upon solvation and a newly developed term that accounts for the response of the environment, which may then be combined with a standard expression for the corresponding change in entropy. In applications to eight neutral solutes in water, internal energies are all found to converge rapidly and in a smooth manner upon an increase in the size of the solvated cluster, and the corresponding enthalpies and free energies of hydration are likewise found to agree with experimental references within statistical uncertainty.

2610.38565.abstract: 1,3,5-Trioxane, a polyoxymethylene (POM) molecule relevant to prebiotic chemistry and astrophysics, exhibits a dense rovibrational spectrum that challenges high-resolution spectroscopic characterization. Here, we report an extensive study of its $ν$ 5 CO symmetric stretching mode (960-1000 cm -1 ) by combining broadband high-resolution FTIR spectroscopy (0.001 cm -1 resolution, >2000 transitions) with SI-traceable sub-Doppler saturated absorption measurements using frequency-stabilized CO 2 lasers and a frequency-comb-referenced quantum cascade laser. The latter achieve lineposition uncertainties as low as 40 kHz, revealing inaccuracies in the FTIR frequency scale. A frequency-scale correction is determined by maximizing the global consistency of the complete spectroscopic data set. A global least-squares Hamiltonian fit combining the calibrated FTIR data, the SI-traceable sub-Doppler measurements and previously reported millimeter-wave rotational transitions yields a refined spectroscopic model. The resulting analysis significantly improves the precision of the rotational, quartic, and sextic constants for both the ground and $ν$ 5 excited vibrational states. This work extends mid-infrared frequency metrology to the largest molecule studied to date (12 atoms), providing a dense set of reference transitions for frequency calibration around 970 cm -1 . The resulting spectroscopic parameters reach relative uncertainties as low as 3.7 x 10 -10 for the band origin, making them valuable for molecular databases used in astrophysics and atmospheric physics, as well as for precision measurements in fundamental physics. Additionally, the observed line shapes indicate the absence of significant intramolecular vibrational energy redistribution (IVR) within the investigated energy range, while a few discrepancies in the Hamiltonian fit suggest the onset of weak perturbations, demonstrating the sensitivity of the present approach to probe subtle intramolecular couplings in complex polyatomic spectra. 2610.38565.title: Extending the limits of rotationally resolved mid-IR spectroscopy: an accurate model of trioxane derived from combining Fourier transform and sub-Doppler measurements

2610.38937.abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. More broadly, the potential enables reactive simulations of diamond, silicon nitride and silica with near-ab initio accuracy at length and time scales beyond first-principles methods, providing a useful tool for future studies of wear at plowing asperities, chemical-mechanical polishing, and properties of amorphous ceramic films.
2610.38937.title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load

2610.39513.abstract: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.
2610.39513.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties

2610.39623.abstract: Paramagnetic color centers in silicon are being investigated recently for use in quantum technologies. While the origin of most of the prominent photoluminescence (PL) lines are well understood, that is not the case for those connected to hydrogen, even though it is almost always present in silicon, e.g., shallow hydrogen-related donors (SHDs), but their atomic structure remains elusive. Recent experiments suggested connection between the SHDs and the so-called X and the B$_i$ (or X$_i$) PL-lines. An SHD, termed the MT2 center, was tentatively assigned to a bistable, negative-U defect, arising due to the interaction of hydrogen with the self-interstitial complex I$_4$. Using high-level density functional theory calculations, we investigate the interaction of hydrogen with self-interstitial complexes In. A shallow effective-mass-theory donor arises when hydrogen attacks a Si-Si bond in I$_n$, inserting itself as a bond-center interstitial (I$_n$H$_{BC}$) in an exothermic reaction. We demonstrate this in the case of a single self-interstitial and of a complex of four. The latter I$_\mathrm{4}$H$_\mathrm{BC}$ complex shows electronic, spin and PL properties remarkably close to MT2. We find that hydrogen in the presence of I$_4$ follows the same behavior as in pristine silicon, i.e., it is a negative-U bistable defect, only detectable under illumination. In the I$_4$H$_{BC}$ complex, H can hop via photo-assisted mechanism between equivalent BC sites of the I$_4$ complex, leading to a motional averaged tetragonal symmetry as experimentally observed for MT2. The zero-phonon line is distinct from the X-line (attributed to the bare I$_4$ complex), and falls well into the range of the X$_i$ lines. Our results identify the I$_4$H complex as a prototype for a class of SHDs, inferring that similar SHDs may arise, with the X$_i$ lines as their PL fingerprints, when H attacks I$_n$ clusters.
2610.39623.title: Origin and photoluminescence of a shallow hydrogen-related donor in silicon

2610.39687.abstract: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

2610.39687.title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency

2610.39713.abstract: Silicon color centers emitting in the near infrared offer a route to spin--photon interfaces compatible with mature complementary metal--oxide--semiconductor fabrication. A key unresolved candidate is the X-line at 1039.7 meV in the photoluminescence (PL) spectrum, long attributed to a complex of four self-interstitials (I$_4$), yet whose microscopic structure and spin properties have remained controversial and uncharacterized at a predictive level. Using hybrid-functional (HSE06) density functional theory, we unambiguously establish the bare I$_4$ complex as the origin of the X-line: our calculations quantitatively reproduce the zero-phonon line, the complete phonon sideband structure---identifying the prominent secondary peaks as one- and two-phonon replicas of strongly coupled quasi-local modes---and the EPR hyperfine constants. The charge transition level is found at VBM$+$0.08~eV, conclusively ruling out the previously proposed association with the B3 EPR center and its correlated deep donor level. Most significantly, we identify a metastable spin-1 triplet excited state separated from the singlet by $\sim$1.6~meV, consistent with the NL51 EPR signal. The $D_{2d}$ symmetry of the defect suppresses intersystem crossing and phosphorescence by first-order spin--orbit coupling, implying an exceptionally long spin--lattice relaxation time. Combined with a spectrally resolvable zero-field splitting and near-infrared emission, the triplet state of the I$_4$ complex constitutes a viable spin quantum memory intrinsic to silicon.
2610.39713.title: I$_4$ complex acting as near-infrared emitter with a quantum memory in silicon

2610.40338.abstract: Electronic grand-canonical density functional theory captures how structure and electronic charge respond to electrode potential and, together with statistical mechanics, how these responses give rise to emergent phenomena. However, its computational cost limits the system sizes and sampling times accessible to first- principles simulations. Here, we introduce a differentiable architecture that represents the grand potential and obtains forces and electronic charge as its derivatives, exactly satisfying the mixed-derivative constraints required for thermodynamic consistency, and implement it within the equivariant MACE framework as GC- MACE. We demonstrate more accurate joint learning across multiple electrochemical interfaces and improved transferability to thicker water films relative to previous models, while enabling constant-potential simulations at substantially larger length and time scales than accessible to ab initio molecular dynamics. With broad training data, the framework offers a route to thermodynamically consistent foundation interatomic potentials for the electronic grand canonical ensemble
2610.40338.title: Differentiable Electronic Grand Canonical Learning for Electrochemistry

2610.40445.abstract: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.
